lead: Partial prestressing is the middle ground between full prestressing and ordinary reinforced concrete. The member carries both tendons and untensioned bars; the tendons supply enough prestress to keep it uncracked under its permanent load, and under the full service load fine, controlled cracks are allowed, which the bars keep narrow. It uses fewer tendons, less camber and simpler end blocks than full prestressing, and gives more ductility. You meet it in building floor beams, parking decks, many bridge decks and precast members where hairline cracks under peak load are acceptable.
prereq: You need the Type 1, 2 and 3 members and the ultimate moment, and crack control from serviceability of reinforced concrete beams.

blocks.text: A fully prestressed member (Type 1 or Type 2) has no tension, or tension below the cracking stress, under the full service load. A partially prestressed member (Type 3) is allowed to crack under the full service load, with the crack width limited; IS 1343 limits it to 0.2 mm for ordinary exposure and 0.1 mm for aggressive exposure. The cracks close again when the live load goes, because the prestress pulls them shut. Reinforced concrete is the other end of the scale, with no prestress at all.

Two numbers describe where a member sits on that scale. The degree of prestressing compares the decompression moment with the service moment, λ = Mdec/Ms: λ ≥ 1 is full prestressing, 0 < λ < 1 partial, λ = 0 reinforced concrete. The partial prestressing ratio compares the strengths of the two steels at ultimate:

blocks.where: A<sub>p</sub> f<sub>pb</sub> is the tendon force and A<sub>s</sub> 0.87f<sub>y</sub> the force in the untensioned bars at the ultimate limit state, both in N. PPR = 1 for full prestressing, 0 for reinforced concrete.

items: Full prestressing designed for a live load that rarely acts gives a large permanent camber, which can grow with creep and crack floor finishes.
Fewer tendons mean fewer anchorages, ducts and end-block links, and a cheaper, quicker job.
The untensioned bars add ductility and warning before failure, which full prestressing with few, highly stressed tendons can lack.
The bars can be placed where they are most useful: over supports, at openings, and for crack control near the faces.

blocks.text: The price is that the member is cracked under peak load: its stiffness is lower then, the tendon stress varies more, which matters for fatigue in bridges, and the crack width must be checked. Partial prestressing is not a weak form of full prestressing; it is a deliberate choice for members whose live load is a large, occasional part of the total.

items: Choose the prestress to balance the permanent load or to give decompression under the quasi-permanent load, using the effective force after losses.
At transfer, check the stresses with P<sub>i</sub> as for any prestressed member.

At service, find the tension under the full load; if it exceeds the cracking stress, the member is Type 3 and the crack width must be checked on the cracked section (IS 1343 gives limiting hypothetical tensile stresses as a simpler check).

At ultimate, put both steels in the force balance: 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> = A<sub>p</sub> f<sub>pb</sub> + A<sub>s</sub> 0.87f<sub>y</sub>, and take moments about the compression with each steel at its own depth.
Check that both steels have yielded, using strain compatibility, and check deflection and shear.

examples.question: A floor beam 300 mm × 650 mm of M40 concrete has four 12.7 mm strands (98.7 mm² each, f<sub>p</sub> = 1860 N/mm², effective stress 1116 N/mm²) at d<sub>p</sub> = 550 mm, and three 16 mm Fe 500 bars at d<sub>s</sub> = 600 mm. The service moment is 260 kN·m. Find (a) the degree of prestressing and the bottom stress at service, (b) the ultimate moment and the PPR, and (c) the number of strands full prestressing would need at the same eccentricity.
steps: Bottom stress at service = 2.259 + 4.693 − 12.308 = −5.36 N/mm², a tension of 5.36 N/mm² against f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7√40 = 4.43: the beam cracks under full load, so it is Type 3 and the crack width must be checked.
x<sub>u</sub> = 901,251/(0.36 × 40 × 300) = 208.6 mm. Strains: tendon 0.0115 (well past elastic); bars 0.0035 × (391.4/208.6) = 0.0066 ≥ 0.00417, so both steels yield.
(c) Zero tension at 260 kN·m needs P<sub>e</sub> ≥ 260 × 10⁶/(108.33 + 225) = 780 kN, that is 780/110.15 = 7.08 → 8 strands.
examples.answer: λ = 0.56: the beam decompresses at 147 kN·m and has 5.36 N/mm² tension at 260 kN·m, so it is partially prestressed (Type 3). M<sub>u</sub> = 430 kN·m with PPR = 0.71. Full prestressing would need 8 strands instead of 4, twice the prestressing steel, with a much larger camber under the permanent load.

traps: Calling partial prestressing a lower grade of full prestressing. It is a deliberate choice, with its own checks for crack width and fatigue.
Adding the tendon and bar moments without checking that both steels have yielded. Use strain compatibility; the lever arms are different.
Using the gross section for stresses after the beam has cracked. Crack width and stiffness need the cracked section.
Forgetting losses in the service check: the degree of prestressing uses P<sub>e</sub>, not the jacking force.
Mixing up the two ratios: λ is a service quantity (moments), PPR an ultimate one (steel forces).

quiz.a: Prestressing in which the member is allowed to crack under the full service load, with the crack width limited by untensioned bars working together with the tendons (Type 3).

quiz.q: What crack widths does IS 1343 allow for Type 3 members?
quiz.a: 0.2 mm for ordinary exposure and 0.1 mm for aggressive exposure.

quiz.q: Why can full prestressing be a poor choice for a floor carrying a heavy but occasional live load?
quiz.a: The prestress needed to stop tension under the rare full load gives a large camber and high compression for most of the member's life, and needs many tendons and anchorages.

quiz.q: Why do the cracks in a partially prestressed member close after the live load is removed?
quiz.a: Under the permanent load the prestress keeps the section in compression, so when the live load goes the tendon pulls the crack faces back together.

quiz.q: A member has M<sub>dec</sub> = 150 kN·m and a service moment of 200 kN·m. Find λ and classify it.
quiz.a: λ = 150/200 = 0.75; between 0 and 1, so it is partially prestressed and may crack under the full load.

quiz.q: A section has tendons with A<sub>p</sub> f<sub>pb</sub> = 600 kN and bars with A<sub>s</sub> 0.87f<sub>y</sub> = 300 kN at ultimate. Find the PPR.
In the worked example, the bars are removed and nothing else changes. What happens at service and at ultimate?
quiz.a: At service the decompression moment stays 147 kN·m, but the cracks at 260 kN·m are no longer held narrow by bars. At ultimate only the tendon force 639 kN remains: x<sub>u</sub> = 147.9 mm and M<sub>u</sub> = 311.7 kN·m, a loss of 118 kN·m.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer codes no longer use the word partial prestressing much; they treat every member as reinforced concrete with some prestress and check stress and crack width limits for each exposure class. Fatigue of strands at cracked sections is a design check for railway bridges. Search for degree of prestressing, partial prestressing ratio and crack width in prestressed members.
